facts.claim: The single 'Hallelujah (Live from St. Mark's Cathedral)' by Noah Gundersen was released on August 19, 2022. The track runs about 5:52.
The release is credited as ℗ 2022 80BPM LLC under exclusive licence to Cooking Vinyl America LLC.
Gundersen performed 'Hallelujah' as a Leonard Cohen cover at a concert at Saint Mark's Episcopal Cathedral in Seattle on December 4, 2021.
The December 4, 2021 St. Mark's Cathedral show was announced as a live performance of his album A Pillar of Salt in its entirety.
A Pillar of Salt (2021) is Gundersen's sixth studio album. It was released by Cooking Vinyl America on October 8, 2021, and produced by Andy Park.

A companion single from the same cathedral recording, 'Sleepless in Seattle (Live from St. Mark's Cathedral)', was also released in 2022. 'Sleepless in Seattle' is Gundersen's own song, first released September 10, 2021.
Gundersen was born in Olympia and raised in Centralia, Washington. He was home-schooled by conservative, religious parents, left home at 18, and started playing around Seattle.
In 2008, Gundersen and his sister Abby formed the band The Courage. The band played until 2011, when he focused on a solo singer-songwriter career.
His 2014 self-produced full-length debut was Ledges. It followed a series of solo EPs, including 2011's Family.
Gundersen has said his work is primarily autobiographical and that he makes music for himself first. He described songwriting as a therapeutic process.

research.lineage: A solo live cover of Leonard Cohen's 'Hallelujah', recorded in a Seattle cathedral, by a Pacific Northwest indie-folk singer-songwriter whose work often deals with faith and doubt.

draft:
A second voice slides in under the title word, low and close, and the cathedral takes both of them and holds the sound a beat longer than either singer does. That held note is the whole argument of Noah Gundersen's **Hallelujah - Live from St. Mark's Cathedral**: a song of praise sung in a room built for praise, by someone who grew up inside that language and walked out of it.

The facts make the setting matter. Gundersen was raised in Centralia, Washington, home-schooled by conservative, religious parents, and left home at 18 to play around Seattle. On December 4, 2021, he played Saint Mark's Episcopal Cathedral in Seattle, a show announced as a full performance of his sixth album, A Pillar of Salt. Leonard Cohen's song came along that night as a cover. A companion recording of his own "Sleepless in Seattle" came out of the same evening. He has called his work mostly autobiographical and described songwriting as therapy. Put those pieces together and a cover becomes something more personal. He isn't borrowing a church song. He's bringing an old vocabulary back into the building where it lives and seeing whether it still fits.

The arrangement doesn't try to answer that question. An acoustic guitar picks out arpeggiated chords, the tone clean and bright, never strummed hard. The tempo is slow and unhurried, close to the pace of someone thinking out loud. Gundersen's voice is clear and sustained, and he leans on long notes rather than pushing for volume. The harmony voice arrives on the refrain and doesn't crowd it. Nothing else is in the mix: just strings, two voices, and a lot of air. The room reverb is the third instrument, and it makes the recording feel raw and close even as the space opens out behind it.

That restraint is the right call. This is a song people tend to perform as a climb toward a big release. Here the release comes from the stone walls, not the singer. Gundersen sings the word plainly and lets the cathedral decide how much weight it carries. What he feels about it stays in the delivery, steady and careful. Reverence and distance sit side by side, and he doesn't settle which one wins.

The second voice matters for the same reason. Praise sung alone can sound like a private wrestling match. With a harmony under it, it becomes something shared, even if each singer means something different by it.

You hear a person stand in a church and say the oldest word in the room without being sure what it means to him anymore, and the building gives it back to you, softer and longer, as if it still believes for both of you.
